name: TV size and distance
seoTitle: TV size and distance Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: TV size and distance: a free other calculator that walks you through 7 values, with the formula spelled out and a worked example.
summary: The TV size and distance calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports minimal distance immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer. It suits whatever you happen to be working on. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the TV size and distance calculator work?
sections.html:
The TV size and distance calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports minimal distance in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the resolution).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 6 options, such as 480p, 720p and 1080p. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Display screen width and viewing angle”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the TV size and distance calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Minimal distance=(8 ÷ 337) × the square root of (337) × screen diagonal length ÷ the tangent of ((1 ÷ 21600) × PI × resolution)
Minimal distance=(1 ÷ 2) × screen width ÷ the tangent of ((1 ÷ 21600) × PI × resolution)
Optimal distance=(8 ÷ 337) × the square root of (337) × screen diagonal length ÷ the tangent of ((1 ÷ 2) × viewing angle)
Screen width=2 × optimal distance × the tangent of ((1 ÷ 2) × viewing angle)
Screen width=(16 ÷ 337) × the square root of (337) × screen diagonal length

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Resolution set to 1080p, Screen diagonal length = 30 cm, Viewing angle = 30 deg and Minimal distance = 30 m. The calculator returns Screen width = 17.2047 cm and Optimal distance = 48.791 m.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Screen width = 17.2047 cm and Optimal distance = 48.791 m should be roughly the size you expected from Resolution set to 1080p and Screen diagonal length = 30 cm.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The TV size and distance calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the TV size and distance calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns minimal distance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the TV size and distance calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter screen diagonal length in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Screen diagonal length opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Screen width = 17.2047 cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the TV size and distance calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
